text: It's an amazing amount of social coordination to get from rough consensus among that tiny community of scientists to enough trust that 240 million people will try a new kind of vaccine to protect against a new kind of virus they don't have experience with.

author: jachiam0
text: Let's say these are vast underestimates and the community of experts in this space has ~50,000 highly-trained people who have rough consensus. My alma mater has a higher total enrollment than that.

author: jachiam0
text: A quick Google search yields numbers like "9,136: Number of infectious disease specialists in the United States" (from WebMD), 2611 for number of members in the American Society for Virology.

author: jachiam0
text: But how many people are experts in virology? How many people are experts in mRNA vaccine design? How many people are legitimately qualified to have high levels of certainty that this works as-described, that the safety and efficacy studies are sufficiently exhaustive?

author: jachiam0
text: And in many sub-disciplines, the answers that people come up with are very reliably testable and correct. And scientists will get it right, fast, when lives are on the line.

author: jachiam0
text: For those of us who are in science, maybe it's a little easier: we know that for all the faults in the scientific community, for all the issues with peer review, for all the poorly-designed incentives in academia, science tends to march on to the correct answer.

author: jachiam0
text: And make no mistake: it's a *huge* amount of uncertainty. "Trust the science" is a difficult slogan to rely on when you ask hundreds of millions of people to accept an injection designed and understood only by a very tiny group of experts.

author: jachiam0
text: I know a lot of folks are bummed about militant anti-vaxxers and the anti-vax grifters, but it's worth celebrating that in the USA more than 72% of people have at least one dose. That's a remarkable amount of social coordination in the face of high uncertainty.

author: jachiam0
text: Let Greg be Greg. Don't force or pressure anyone to be Greg. Reward people for working in ways that create high quality results and are sustainable for them, whether or not that looks like your personal preference.

author: jachiam0
text: But we also create a bad culture when we punish people who are otherwise performing well for having working styles that don't line up with our own preferences and expectations.

author: jachiam0
text: Different people have different working styles. We create bad cultures when we start overly rewarding people for working in unsustainable ways, or requiring it, or glorifying it, or subtly punishing people for not doing it.

author: jachiam0
text: And I've seen folks sometimes totally ignore all of that advice because they were crazy excited by the problem they were working on. They were getting something out of it.

author: jachiam0
text: I've been at OpenAI for years, and I've always stressed to colleagues, mentees, and reports the importance of thinking of work as a marathon and not as a sprint---that they should take time they need to breathe, not work on weekends, not overdo it, take a day off if needed.

author: jachiam0
text: My experience whenever I've put in more than 40 hours in a week wasn't that I did it because I was told to or because it was normalized or glorified, but because I was working on problems I couldn't stop thinking about because they were important to me.

author: jachiam0
text: My experience inside OpenAI's culture is a lot more balanced than @dlowd's tweet suggests. People value hard work but not overwork and overwork/burnout is seen as a sign that a project needs more support. It's far from perfect but no one is asked to be Greg.

author: jachiam0
text: Some people feel intensely motivated by what they're working on and would gladly put as many waking hours as they could into it, because that would maximize their life satisfaction. Those people should be free to do it. They shouldn't be punished for it.

author: jachiam0
text: Absolutely no one should have to work a 90 hour week and no one should feel obligated to. But I also think it's weird to police how many hours people work if they're doing what they want to do.

author: jachiam0
text: Greg's personal take is that working a 90 hour week is helping him make progress. He's not saying literally everyone has to do that to be valuable. He's not asking for exploitative labor practices. He's doing this because he enjoys it and because it's how he gets results.

author: jachiam0
text: Ilya said you have to work hard to make progress in AI, obviously true. Making progress on hard problems requires hard work in general---sometimes you can pull a fast one on a hard problem but that's the exception, not the rule. He didn't say you have to work 90 hour weeks.

author: jachiam0
text: Some thoughts: it's harmful to say "You have to work 90 hours per week to be successful," because that normalizes the idea that everyone has to do it. But that's not quite what's happening here and this strikes me as a bit disingenuous.
